finding: nothing caps how many refs one run may put on the owner's desk, and the count doubled past every prior run without any signal

WHAT WE LEARNED: the framework has a cap on BUILDS (capBuilds) and none on DECISIONS, yet decisions are the scarce resource - they are the only step that cannot be parallelised, batched or delegated, because there is one owner. A run that dispatches 100 fixes and asks him nothing is cheap; a run that dispatches 8 and asks him 25 questions is unfollowable, and the engine currently cannot tell those two apart. The engine already knows the number - it assembles the report - so this is a count and a warning, not a new mechanism, and it composes with X30: routing discoveries to intake is what brings 25 back under the budget without dropping anything. WHY NOT JUST A CAP: silently truncating to the first N would be the no-silent-caps failure. It must report what it held back and why. OBSERVABLE: the manifest prints refs-on-his-desk against the trailing average, and says so out loud when a run exceeds it - so the shape of yesterday would have been visible at 17:20 instead of at 23:50. RISK: a budget invites gaming by merging unrelated rows into one to stay under it, which is worse than 25 honest rows. The budget must trigger a warning and a deferral proposal, never a merge.

finding: the scout brief makes a ticket's TITLE the symptom and demotes its body to evidence, so a ticket listing three complaints yields one issue

Neither was a drop: droppedAsOpenKnown was gh#155 and gh#154 only, droppedAsAlreadyBuilt was empty.
note: WHAT WE LEARNED: the owner writes tickets as a pasted Slack transcript followed by a numbered list of what went wrong - gh#156 ends with 1. why first going to online or person 2. why she lied 3. what does getting back to you mean. That numbered list IS the work. The brief instructs the scout to treat the title as the symptom, so the list becomes supporting evidence for a single title-shaped issue, and two of the three complaints were never surfaced by any run. They reached report.md as rows 173 and 174 only at 00:18 when the OWNER named them himself, and report.md records the consequence in its own words: gh#156's other two complaints, which no scout has ever surfaced. WHY THIS SOLUTION: one line of the brief, inverted - enumerate the complaints in the body FIRST and emit one issue per complaint, then use the title only as a label for the group. The atomic-split rule the scout charter already holds then does the rest. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND gh#156: this is also why every ticket ended PARTIAL and nothing could close. Three tickets went in, each with three complaints, and the run engaged with one complaint per ticket. OBSERVABLE: the scout reports complaintsFound per ticket against issuesEmitted, so 3-in-1-out is visible in the manifest rather than invisible until the owner reads the ticket himself. RISK: a body with a long transcript and no numbered list has no complaints to enumerate, and forcing a count there would invent issues. The rule must be enumerate what is explicitly listed, never infer a list that is not there.

finding: when the scout merges a GitHub ticket with a log moment the merged row loses the ticket number, so ticket coverage cannot be computed for it
evidence: In wf_33541300-121 the two single-source rows kept their parent - 158-attendee-misresolution and 157-calendar-filter-and-history-gap - while the one row with source both became flow-narrates-unexecuted-actions with no 156 anywhere in it. gh#158 therefore got an explicit coverage row reading TICKET COVERAGE: partial - do NOT close #158 on this wave, and gh#156 got none, because no ref in the run named it.
note: WHAT WE LEARNED: this is the more dangerous half of the scout problem, because it is silent in a way X32 is not. X32 loses complaints; this loses the LINK, and once the link is gone nothing downstream can notice anything is missing. The coverage check is not broken - it worked perfectly for gh#158 - it simply had no row to fire on for gh#156. That is the framework's signature failure shape once more: a mechanism that does nothing and looks exactly like success, because a ticket with no coverage row is indistinguishable from a ticket with nothing wrong. WHY THIS SOLUTION: make the parent ref structural rather than conventional. A merged row keeps the ticket ref and gains the log evidence, so source both means both sources are named, not that the weaker id wins. This is also the same fix the owner proposed independently for dependency numbering - see the sibling row on report ids - and the two should be built as one change, because both are the rule that every id derives from its parent. WHY IT IS CHEAP: the ledger ALREADY does parent-scoped refs correctly (gh#158-exception-must-be-name-scoped), so the convention exists and is proven; only the merge path departs from it. OBSERVABLE: every ticket named in the scout's input appears in at least one ref in the run's output, and the manifest lists any ticket that does not. Run against yesterday, gh#156 appears. RISK: forcing a parent onto a genuinely source-less log finding would create fake ticket links. The rule applies only where a ticket was actually merged in.

finding: report row ids are a flat counter, so a blocker raised on a ticket gets an unrelated number and the ids collide with GitHub issue numbers
evidence: state.json nextReportId is 175 and yesterday's rows were 160-174, while the ledger refs for the same work are parent-scoped (gh#158-exception-must-be-name-scoped). Report rows 164 and 165 existed at the same time as gh#164 and gh#165, filed 2026-07-29 at 18:24 and 18:30, and the owner rules by bare number - 165 - lets ignore it.
note: OWNER'S DESIGN, in his words: if you had ticket 153 and you got something that block it, it won't be 170, it will be 153-blockA or something. WHAT WE LEARNED: there are two id systems and they disagree. The ledger already uses parent-scoped refs and gets this right; the REPORT uses a flat counter, and the report is the surface he actually reads and rules on. So the good convention exists in the place nobody looks and the bad one is in the place where decisions are made. Three separate problems collapse into this one change. First, a raised blocker becomes traceable at a glance - 153-blockA says what it blocks, 170 says nothing. Second, coverage becomes arithmetic rather than prose: a ticket with three complaints that emitted 156-a only is VISIBLY incomplete without anyone writing a coverage sentence, which is what failed for gh#156. Third, the collision with GitHub numbers disappears, because 156-a can never be mistaken for an issue number while 165 always can. WHY THIS SOLUTION AND NOT A PREFIX: a prefix like R165 would fix only the collision and would leave the parent unnamed, so it solves the smallest of the three. WHY IT IS SAFE: the counter's own rule - never renumber, never reuse - is preserved by keeping the flat sequence for rows with no parent, and only rows derived from a ticket or from another row take the derived form. OBSERVABLE: no report row id is a bare integer that also exists as an open GitHub issue number, and every child row's id contains its parent's. RISK: state.json's nextReportId note says ids must be stable forever because 14 must mean the same thing next month. Migrating existing rows would break that, so this applies to NEW rows only and the flat ones keep their numbers.

The report does not need to hold the rows, only to state the true number and where to see them, so at minimum the wrap must never print a zero it did not compute. OBSERVABLE: the number in report.md's headline equals the number ledger-stats --open returns, checkable in one command at any moment. finding: a finished run wakes the chat and the chat stays silent, so a completed wave can sit unread for hours

WHY THIS SOLUTION: one PushNotification call in the Manager's post-run protocol, carrying the count that matters - refs on his desk, tickets touched, whether a verify is still owed. Not a new mechanism; a tool that already exists and has never once been called. OBSERVABLE: the gap between a run's return timestamp and his first turn on it, which is measurable from any transcript and was 252 minutes yesterday. RISK: a push per lane return would be noise.
